I purchased a Leite model LT1012, a 1.2 ton mini excavator with all the attachments from China. The China price was $4500. The dozens of fees to get it to my door cost an additional $4700! So it actually costs $200 more to get it from the port in LA to Pahrump Nevada than the cost of the machine from China to the USA. $1300 of this was thanks to Trump's tariffs on China. However, the quality of the machine is excellent. It is constructed with robust steel and very nice welding. But there is no after-market support. They cannot even supply a service manual. I have only been able to learn how to service the machine by watching YouTube videos!

comments.author: @court2379
comments.text:
Neat products and I am excited to see what is being produced, but the use if lead acid batteries is a terrible design flaw. See if you can get them to switch to lithium for future imports. 
Lead acid batteires limit the useful time severely, and degrade quickly. Meaning they will need to be replaced in 5 years, and the performance of the unit will be half or less of new in only a couple years. Charge times will be really long as well.

People also need to be aware how poorly they will perform in below freezing temperatures.

Really a hybrid would be ideal. The fuel motor can heat the batteries up in the cold and keep the useful range/time up in general. It can be switched off for quiet work when it is warm enough.

comments.text:
Great video! As much as some will hate to hear this, this is an honest to goodness example of China's clear manufacturing superiority. Great innovative useful machines, at half the price, with all of the benefits of electrification, great engineering, sturdy, etc. 
In fairness, we didn't see it load a dump truck, or do heavy work in a tough rocky or muddy construction or mining worksite, but for $20k-$30K for a new loader that can work an  8-hour day of intermittent use, its a better product. 
I assume air conditioning (AC), universal skid-steer mounts,  and bullet-proof cabin glass are available, but those things cost money - and AC is going to reduce running time. It costs $1000 per day in fuel to run a lot of equipment, so fuel is not a small savings here, it's a huge savings - especially when the cost of the loader is cheaper as well.
It would be interesting to see the specs and comparison of how that drivetrain keeps up with a diesel loader - on a construction worksite.

comments.author: @rf_dude
comments.text: Nice subjective show.  Objective (numbers) are found in your sales web site under technical specifications.  SHOW the battery and internal pumps/hydraulics please.  Battery gas gauge (voltage and capacity left)?  How big of a job with near continuous use was the battery tested?  When the battery fails in 5 years, is the battery space friendly to substitutes and "best fit" or what will fit in the space?   Based on 72V at 14.4kWh,  this would require 6 blocks x 12V 200 AHr which would be 6 x $400 to replace.  Here is the challenge... the battery replacement cost is an equivalent substitute for the fuel and oil change costs that would have poured through a diesel engine over that equivalent battery life.   That's assuming the battery lasts 5 years of reasonable use.  Batteries can go bad sooner if left unattended or not topped up (AGM or SLA (lead battery) is best left in float...  100% charged) when stored.  Do not store partially discharged.   Please show the devilish technical/objective details please.  It is all workable, just need to present more of the technical trade-off's and comparables. Words provide context, but answers are in the numbers.  Good luck in your ventures.

One of the best ways to get past the damage issues in transit is to order at least one extra machine as spares. Breaking a whole machine for spare parts is often more cost effective than buying the spares individually from the manufacturer and covers your potential major component warranty service provision. comments.text:
How does such an amateurish kludge get so many likes and views?!

Critical safety and professional violations:

* No inspection waives the requirement to have proper permits for working on real electrical equipment, even in your own home.
* Cutting wire insulation incorrectly with a knife across the wire.
* Lack of proper tools – extremely unsafe knife handling with a high risk of injury.
* Improper panel mounting: The panel width is 14.25", while the space between structural supports exceeds 14.5". Forcing installation without using compensating spacers deforms the panel, which will lead to issues with deadfront, door, latch, and other components.
* Phase connection order is critical – it must comply with the manufacturer’s specifications.
* Using a single hex wrench is insufficient – torque-specific tools are required as per manufacturer guidelines.
...
I had to stop watching – the sheer number of professional errors is overwhelming. There are likely even more mistakes beyond this point. Maybe another electrician will have the time (and patience) to watch to the end and point out the rest....

Why is that box so freaking high... 😂
Some adults are short.

A few tips ... 
1: Connect the ground wire first and right under where your hot wire will go into the breaker so you don't have to look around for it later if things need to change ...
Also looks more neat
.
B: run the wire group down to where you would connect to the bottom most breaker .
Again if it needs to be moved later  you have enough slack ..
You already had the wire long enough to do it..

comments.text:
With the ground wire sitting bare in the ground, won't it be eaten away by oxidation pretty quickly, to the point where you need to replace it every 10 or so years?

Here in Sweden, the only permitted ways of running cable in the ground is to either use cable that has armoring and a weather and water proof outer sheathing, or run your sheathed and insulated cables in fit-for-purpose plastic tubing put down into the ground, which then is sealed water-tight. That way, your cables will reliably last for 50+ years while maintaining a very low ground impedance.

comments.text:
I've always seen sub panel breakers placed away from the rest of the house breakers when the main panel box is big enough to make them quickly identifiable. 
Even for people that don't know how electric services work, having it away from other breakers draws their attention to the "out of place" location so they know something is different about that breaker. 
I've also seen boxes where the electrician took the section of sheathing that the run was marked for and reinsert it onto the run but left it on fire final installation of the circuit for future reference. This is especially helpful if the panel is ever upgraded.

comments.text: Code says coat individual strands of aluminum wires with oxidation inhibitor... work it down into the ends of the wires so current can flow between strands.  Most inspectors will want to see the tips of those wires above those terminal blocks to make sure the contact area is not too small.  Are you sure the hot water heater doesn't require GFCI?  Aluminum subpanel wires should have oxidation inhibitor coating...  ALL aluminum wires should have oxidation inhibitor coating their junctions.  Aluminum oxide (sapphire) is very hard and has very high resistivity; high resistance connections get hot and start fires.  The panel cover must be off for the drywall crew...  I saw one crew install drywall on top of the panel cover edges.

comments.text: Great video! There are a couple of things that you need to change up though for future reference. First, it is required to torque the Main Lugs to the specified in-lbs indicated on the panel. (Yes, I know all screws are supposed to be torqued now but the Main Lugs are especially important.)  Secondly, not knowing your AHJ and the fact they probably haven't adopted the 2020 code yet, but you will need to install a service disconnect before your main panel. This is code now and when it is adopted you will put that homeowner behind the curve if they ever need to have the panel upgraded/etc. This also means that the main panel will be a sub panel and the grounds and neutrals will have to be separate and bonded together in the main disconnect.

comments.author: @shambles3833
comments.text:
I think a lot of these videos and articles miss the gap when they're trying to appeal to layman like myself.  While the video does talk about the difference between the electrical path returning via the neutral, when operations are proper, vs the ground wire, say when the metal chassis becomes energized, it doesn't quite cover the confusion as to why that matters when it's the same copper wires travelling back to the panel where they are connected.  At first when the video talked about the ground wire having a very low resistance, hence causing a quick spike in current (amps) that cause the breaker to flip, that still doesn't make sense to a newbie as we are looking at the neutral and ground wires and telling ourselves that they are made of the same copper, so they should have the same resistance.  What we, the ignorant, fail to consider is that when an electrical load is sent through the hot wire, into say a light fixture, and returns on the neutral, that the light acts as a resistor, hence why the neutral line has a much higher resistance than the ground line.

This leads me to a follow up question. comments.text: Not to be that guy but ground wires are never less resistance than neutral. Commercial wiring you generally use the conduit which has far greater resistance than copper.  In house wiring they use the same gauge so it is easier to work with. Anything larger than 12GA will generally have a ground conductor up to 2 sizes smaller (6 Gauge generally has an 8 Gauge ground). The design is to provide 10x rated current flow for enough time to trip the breaker.  So yes path back to the bonding bar but not because it has less resistance.

comments.text: Neutral wires CAN CARRY CURRENT as a matter of course (neutral and load/hot/black wire are the same when that happens).  The difference between the white and black wire is the black wire carries current from the source (panel, power company) to the circuits (behind each breaker).  The white or neutral wire carries that current from the circuit back to the neutral bus (at the panel) which is in turn grounded (completing the circuit path).  So then why have a ground wire?  The ground wire ONLY carries current when a short occurs in the circuit...at that point the electrons are quickly dispatched to ground to stop the flow into YOU or into something not intended to be part of the circuit like a break in a wire touching a nail etc.

This is how I understand it.

When a ground line gets connected to a hot wire. The current flows from the hot wire to ground because there is difference of potential. The definition of current is the flow of charge from high potential to low potential, it does not take into account whether a complete circuit has been formed or not. Sometimes there is nearer, large, difference of potential in the clouds themselves, so the lighting "spiders" across the clouds.

comments.text:
I think there was one misconception on this. If i remember correctly, the ground is actually to prevent EMP energy from things like lightning bolts from frying someone closeby aswell as other benefits they produce, not to directly funnel a lightning strike. A grounding system is NOT lightning protection. 

An ungrounded system may actually be less likely to shock you in the typical manner because in most cases you would have to touch both neutral and line in order to receive a shock. The grounding rod we drive in the ground gives the electricity alternative paths back to the source (like the dirt itself or a pipe or what have you) so that if you touch only line and something grounded at same time you will get a shock. If the neutral and ground wire were not connected at the main panel then that wouldn't happen (for most cases)

This is the reason why equipment grounding is so important. Most of the time these wires are not accessible and should something fail, and the line makes contact with some metal casing then that casing becomes energized and whoever touches it and something grounded will receive a shock (which you mentioned).

Electricity takes ALL viable paths to the source not just one. Also if I understand correctly, the farther you are from a ground rod that has a ground fault occurring, the lower the resistance due to exponentially increasing paths through the earth the farther you are away.

comments.text: 6:31 The ground conductor is connected to the positive terminal of the battery. If I were to place my multimeter leads across the ground conductor and the hot wire I should read 1.5 Volts. This is because the ground conductor behaves as an extension of the positive terminal of the battery, even though it is not a part of the circuit, which is why current does not flow through it (under normal circumstances) even though it is attached to the battery. Now, if I were to straddle a load between the ground conductor and hot wire, this would result in a flow of current between the ground and hot conductors and (hopefully) trip the GFCI in a residential scenario. Please correct me if I have misspoken.

comments.text: I think the video is fine, but I didn't really like the ground explanation as being there so that in an accident, the current knows where to go.   To me, the ground wire *anchors* the surrounding metal at 0V because it's connected to the ground through a wire with no current (vs. the neutral wire which has current and develops a voltage due to the IR drop of the wire).   Surrounding metal could find itself at small (or large) voltages due to parasitic inductance, etc all the time, creating a hazard.   And then you can add that if there's a problem, that voltage can't develop on the case because of the short path to ground via the safety wire.

comments.text:
It is also how it *should* be done. When something is done the proper way, then it is the safest way.

For example, I recently had to install a ceiling fan in my room. Turns out, my room is the only one in the entire house wired wrong. While things still work, it’s prone to potential headaches in the future when it comes to installing things. Such as I cannot have one switch for the fan, and the other for the light, as well as working in the wires is more prone to shock you (which my father found out when it sparked and flipped the circuit breaker in two rooms while working on the switch on the wall).

So… is it easier to just put the things in there since no one really seems them? Yes. Is it the right and safest way to do it like that? No. Also it’s common curtesy for the next person. Because if the last people who worked on my room, it was clear the wiring was an after thought, thus making it MUCH harder to put a simple ceiling fan in, which is already a somewhat tedious thing.

Gee, you saved them the cost of the 6th truck, but insist that, what was saved is to be passed along to you. So, no matter what, the contractor still has to pay for all 6 trucks. 

So tell me, who is stupid enough to make a bet that ends up being a lose lose proposition?

comments.author: @AlanLiefting
comments.text:
Some of these where good but here are my tips in return:
1. Don't use a Philips screwdriver on a Pozidrive screw
2. Don't rely on a knotted wire for safety or reliability.
3. Use a crimp tool for crimps.
4. Stranded wire can be be fastened reliably under a screw and washer if a loop is made with the tail twisted around the bare wire just before where the insulation starts.
5. Apart from aesthetics there is nothing wrong with mains cables being cable ties in a circular manner. (oh, and you should make sure that the plug in the background is pushed in firmly.)
6. Minor point - use side cutters on cable ties.  Scissors are not usually strong enough for cutting cable ties.

comments.text:
To everyone asking why the cable wasnt completely enclosed in the conduit with bends and such: 
In germany electrical wiring needs to be double insulated. In this case the cable itself already is, so in theory he could have just nailed it directly to the walls with some clips, not needing the conduits at all. 
Had he run single wires, then he would have needed to enclose the wires in conduit the whole way. But running single wires in conduit, while allowed, is not usually done here.

Moin! Take a look at the Doepke FIs with short delay on turn on..
still switches off on fault fast enough but allows higher inrush current when for example switching a large pc power supply an three monitors at once.
Come in around 270euros or more, but pretty nice if you dont want to split into multiple Fuse-RCD-combos (DRCBO 3 B16/0,03/1N-A 09932104).
There are also Siemens RCBOs with short delay.. i tend to use Type B RCBOs now instead of Type A
- It's always bad if you switch on the last tool and suddenly are in the dark with spinning blades because everything is behind one RCBO.

(If you want to charge a electric car off that CEE you will need to install a seperate Fuse + separate Type B RCBO or a separate Type A if the wallbox has a DC current sensing)

Soo different:
Separate combination RCBO-Fuses, so only one trips at a time. (maybe type B and delayed type)
Wiring the Emergency-Off the normal way, so you have a power shutoff when you are not using your garage-shed.
(the power consumption isnt what you read, thats the drop/loss at max rated Amps)

Did you get everything tested afterwards ? At least should be done once.

Hello, here is a feedback from Slovenia. First i work in industry and my job is to look electrical installation how it's done and if it is ready for measurements.

First i saw that you use NNY-J cables, can i ask why? We are using cables with mutiple wires inside like FROR or FG16OR16 (i saw that you are using some of this in electical box). Cable with multiple wires inside is better for current and resistance.
 
Are you using same wire for socket and lights? here is not allowed to do that. We alway separate this two because it is different standar.

You showed i picture where you can see that 1,5mm2 can handle 18A,... This is not true, you have three classes for how much curent cable can handle and depends on how good is cooling for cable (where is installed and how). For 1,5mm2 you can use only 12A if im not mistaken but we usually use 10A fuse, for 2,5mm 16A, 20A for 4mm2 and 32A for 6mm2. If cable have better cooling soo it is in cable tray then you can put bigger fuse, exsample for 1,5mm2 18A and cable will heat up to 70°C. 

In electrical box you dont have main switch (here you need to have one). We are not using terminal blocks anymore because more connections is usually bad but it is not wrong at all.
You can put stop press inside a kanal:)

The biggest concern I have about it this would be labeling. Labeling should be priority #2 right after Safety.
Small labels on each outlet and corresponding labeling on the breakers can save an immense amount of work. Even in a 2 room installation, a complete outsider would need to do trial and error (by flicking a breaker) or follow the wires to find breaker/outlet correspondence. This get's exponentially harder on larger objects where the trial and error method might not be an option aswell.

Not a concern but a personal preference would be the use of smaller cable ducts instead of tubes, especially above the distribution box. I think they make it look cleaner and less crowded and are a lot more accessible to modifications than the tubes.

Edit: Another side note, I had an abundance of the Hager-Contactors die on me so I would recommend another brand for them, which in return would make the build less appealing sadly.

comments.text:
Might have been better with a ‘Latching-Contactor’ or Circuit breaker with a ‘Shunt-Trip’ Circuit ?
That would assist with any ‘Fault-Clearing’ operations.
That means the Contactor would stay closed while the Circuit protection clears the circuit fault.

It’s unlikely that there would be a fault at the same time as someone operates the e-stop, but it’s definitely something that’s considered in industrial applications.

Contactors aren’t designed to clear or make fault current, they tend to fail catastrophically when presented with such extremes of Current.

comments.text: ".. I would never recommend a non-professional to do such a job." The problem is professionals make mistakes too. In my house the blue wire is the phase wire and the brown is the neutral. Okay, wrong colors you might think. But as a result of this the switches only break the neutral wire. Meaning when you switch the light off to change the bulb, the socket is still live. At several other houses were "professionals" worked on the wiring the grounds of many sockets were left not connected. Meaning you get a nasty shock if you touch metal housing of the dryer, and the ground fault interrupt won't trip if there's ever a short, for instance due to a leak. My point being: when professionals mess up, it's left to us non-professionals to find the problem and have it fixed.

comments.author: @inothome
comments.text:
Great looking installation and interesting to see how things are done in Germany! Really enjoyed this episode, not that I ever not enjoy your videos. 
The term for an E-Stop or safety mechanism / circuit that opens a circuit when tripped is called "Failsafe". I did go OH NO when I saw your prints, as you said some would. But agreed, in your case it really isn't that important. However, you can install a 240V, low current "pilot light" in parallel with the E-Stop contacts. As long as it's low enough current it will not let the contactor pull in and it will give a visual indication that the relay circuit has continuity. When the E-Stop is pressed it then makes the low resistance path and will operate the relay and pilot light goes out. But, probably not that important for you use, but a pilot light is a low cost, low energy use solution that will verify your relay circuit is good.  Plus, indicator lights are cool!! 
We use the same method in substations for the trip circuit monitor on high voltage breakers. The red "CLOSED" (red = closed in the US) indicator lamp is wired through the trip circuit and trip coil itself and a 52a contact. This way if the breaker is closed and the light is out, it's either a bulb or the trip circuit itself has failed and that IS a big deal in substations!  
Question about using the 4 pole relay / contactor, is it code or normal there to interrupt the neutral? Normally the neutral is never opened in any switching instances, just the hot phases.

comments.author: @dacaca
comments.text:
I like the setup with all this protections (in Spain the electrical setups are similar) and emergency stop switches are so cool, but in my opinion I change a few things: 

1º The wiring, to insert in tubes I prefer individual wires in front of the 3 o 5 wires packed in ruber, with individual wires comply with regulations and it's easy to insert and make future changes (add more wires in the future), and you can add more wires by PVC tube. I watch in the video rigid wires, another thing than I prefer flex coper wires, by the same cross section, more current and make me feel more safe (the rigid wire will broke by the years). 
2º The magnetothermal switches, I prefere 2 poles (P+N) for monophase wiring, and 4 poles (R+S+T+N) for triphase wiring, in your electrical box you only put 3 pole magnetothermal for triphase wiring. Probably is correct, but I prefer to disconnect ALL wirings when switch off in the electrical box.
3º Fuses, I think that is a dangerous thing in 3 phase installation, why? Because if only 1 fuse broken, you can work in 2 phase with 3 phase devices and broken devices (and another catastrophic things, like returns of voltaje in neutral line). For this I prefer a well sized magnetothermal switche with the correct switch curve.
4º I think that you should put emergency lights, I don't know if in Germany it's mandatory for you regulations for your application, but if it isn't, it's recommended because helps you to see in a fault of electricity or if you trip any switch with a faulty device.

But congratulations by your new place to continue doing cool things.

comments.author: @Eytaris
comments.text:
nice video!
A few things, first, I would have limited the use of spring loaded connectors, especially on the 400V, screw terminals may a bit more pain, because they need tightening ideally once a year, but I think they are more secure than spring loaded (if they come loose, you have to replace the whole device).

Adding a few RJ45 sockets in the modular wall conduits wouldn't be too much I think, it's better than trying to catch the Wi-Fi from the house through the concrete walls, plus, that would limit radio emissions too and that would be nice if you try yourself on wireless projects. 

For the emergency stop button, swapping the relay for a security relay is a must, your standard relay doesn't give you the guarantee that it will break the circuit if he got damaged (a short or any type of over-current can easily weld the contacts together) a dedicated security relay will break the circuit permanently if the power module get damaged and the automatic reset of the emergency relay on the NO contacts is a bit risky I think, you have no means to know if the fault still there or a device is still powered, a manual reset next to the door would add the extra step to ensure everything is safe before closing the circuit. I think Schneider make safety relays that include a surveillance module (maybe Häger too, but I don't know their catalog enough), with emergency stop and reset loops and a protected power module that hook the mains right after the fuses and breaker, they are probably more expensive, but I think they worth it.

Just out of curiosity, why the diazed fuses? I thought they were progressively phased out in Europe, is it a standard still very present in Germany? last time I saw this type of fuses, it was on a 30 year old machine, it was a pain to get new fuses and very expensive compared to similar 10x38 cartridges.

That's all I could think of, I hope I didn't come as arrogant or aggressive, English isn't my first language and I was told that sometimes I may come as a bit obnoxious, I assure you it's not my intentions :)

Your video was great for how to make electrical connections in very simple circuits.   Some of your explanations need some polishing.   Couple examples.   It’s not 12/2 and 14/2 Romex. comments.author: @IntenseGrid
comments.text: But do those lever nuts carry as much current?  The wirenuts wrap one copper wire around the other with nothing, and no different metals in between.  The lever nuts, on the other hand connect the wires to what looks like a nickel plated copper making 2 connections to that lever nut metal on the inside instead of direct connection between the wires.  Also the lever nuts probably don't have the same surface area connection between the nut and the wire.  I wouldn't use lever nuts for a 2 wire connection, which the wire nuts excel at, maybe even not a 3 wire connection.  Going beyond 3 wires, however in a wirenut is a real PITA, so I would gladly go to a levernut for 4+ wires.

comments.author: @eatdirtmofo
comments.text: When I was a Kiddie at electrical college, we were taught not to use cable junctions, nor splices whatever, we were taught that every wire had its own place of termination, whether that be the fuse board (consumer unit) or the receptacle. Power was daisy chained (as in ring mains) and spurs were taken from the back of a wall receptacle with a fused unit. Similarly, lighting went to ceiling rose first, then down to switching and back, there were extra terminals in each rose for additional lamps to be added on the same circuit (named loop). There were no mid cable breaks. One of the problems with mid-cable breaks is that they would have to be exposable for inspection, which is fine if you are running exposed conduits, but if running in walls covered by dry-wall and plaster, where do you put the junction box without burying it? Indeed in a lot of Eu countries you will notice circular indentations in the plaster work, that is to show electricians in the future where buried junctions are... Crazy. Going back to College, as we have to every time they upgrade the Regs, I noticed that junction boxes, and mid-cable joints are in favour now, and they even suggest Wagos as the tools to use... How things change, I must be getting old.

comments.author: @telumatramenti7250
comments.text: 2:50 From my own experience - I would not use that "knot" technique, particularly with wires carrying high current, and with something which will be jostled about a lot such as for example a high voltage DC charger for e-mopeds. The "knot" is highly susceptible to thin strands which are closer to the surface breaking off because of the tension its subjected to, and sharp angles. When the individual strands break - then can cut right through the heat shrink tubing. When there's high current going through this wire - these knots tend to heat up more due to higher resistance, and become even more susceptible to losing flexibility, breaking off and cutting through the heat shrink tubing, potentially creating a short circuit which could be unsafe and potentially damage your battery or charger, or cause battery venting and/or fire. Instead, - simply unwind both ends you intend to connect till they look like paint brushes. Dip them in flux, then slowly push the two unwound "bristles" through one another. Now squeeze the joint from all the sides and apply solder with a soldering iron. Something like this will be as strong as the wire itself, yet fairly flexible making it unlikely the little wires will break off and punch through the heat shrink tubing. If the end result still looks uneven, - wipe it with dry tissue and give it some light filing or sanding, but don't overdo it so as not to compromise the thin strands. But make absolutely sure the joint is perfectly smooth before sliding heat shrink sleeve over it.

comments.text:
Great video! Electrician here as well. Just a little 2 cents for anyone interested; since he was using 1/2 inch pipe, the take up (or deduction, the part you subtract when bending a 90 on the arrow) was 5". However, keep in mind, that these change from size to size. So if you're using 3/4" , the deduction is 6". If you're using 1", the deduction is 8". As he said in the video, it will be listed on the bender. Also, if you don't want to do the deduction, you can do something called "bending on center". Usually this is denoted on the bender by a star, and this allows you to just mark your exact measurement, and line the mark up with the star, as opposed to the arrow. Just a little less math involved is all. 

I work mainly commercial, but most of this information was very useful for anyone just starting off/doing a home project. This is stuff i only learned after being at many sites. I've never seen those bracket 1900s though, those are pretty nice!

comments.author: @johnchristmas7522
comments.text: Coming from the UK , this is a fast way to tube an installation. In the UK, tubing is very rare, mainly because of cost and because its all screwed ends. All couplers (joiners) are tapped all the way inside. Just a single screw and push fit would not pass code. All the screwed ends are made using a die or dying machine. All conduit has to be tested for continuity and as the USA ,used for grounding. When entering a fixed box, we use a brass male bush, that pushes through from the inside of the box, screwing straight into a coupler, which has already been screwed onto the tube. Thus reducing ingress of metal fittings into box.The bush is smooth on the rim, so no chaffing of the wires in the box. No. pig tails allowed ever and only ever single phase into any box. Remember we are 240v so two phases in a box is a potential of 415V! I've  had a shock from that-not good! Wiring tube, is done using stranded single cable and if it wired correctly all outlets must never have more than 4 wires. Branching out to another box is seen as bad practice and would leave six wires at on outlet.

comments.text: Having worked in the Electrical Trade, running conduit (EMT $ PVC) , the EMT (Electrical Metallic Tubing), is the more difficult to run. Remember; you have to pull your wires through it and depending on how well you thought it through and did your job correctly, will determine the degree of resistance (friction) you will come up against.  Try to use as LESS bends as possible and obviously, the straighter the conduit run, the easier the wire can be pulled through.  Sometimes, you will require a lubricant (# 11) "wire lubricant compound" to apply with your wire run.  Ensure to REAM your conduit - ALWAYS.  and ensure your connections of your conduit run into the appropriate fittings are secure.  You do not want to have to fail your inspection or have to remove your drywall to fix it.  Work safely.

comments.text:
Some cities and counties in the U.S. require rigid EMT (Electrical Metal Conduit) in situations where the wall cavities are exposed. Wiring needs to be protected from abrasions, or as some people do, hanging objects on the wire.

In basements especially, I have seen everything from clothes hangers, to tools hanging from the Romex/Non-Metallic Cable (NMC) in the joist bays. This is very dangerous! So rigid conduit is used to protect against the wire being damaged and causing a short.

Some jurisdictions allow flex conduit, but only in cases where the flex will be hidden behind a finished wall. Flex is more durable than Romex, but much easier to run than rigid conduit and then having to pull wire.

comments.author: @davenag957
comments.text: A few tips from a guy bending in Chicagoland since 1977. Loose the loaded toolpouch when running pipe. You don't need all that weight slowing you down. All you need are uninsulated 420 channelocks, a screwdriver with a Klein reamer attached, tape measure, pencil and 4 pocket nail apron. You want to be able to work light and fast and have everything you need right in that nail apron. Using a marker is bad for exposed work as it bleeds through paint and you're always having to take the cap off and on the marker which slows you down. Upgrade to a small battery impact for mounting boxes and tightening fittings. Wear sturdy shoes or your right foot will kill you at the end of the day from the bender. Get a short radius bender as you may need it for close quarter work. I used a hand hacksaw thirty-plus years. It killed my shoulder. If you're going to do a lot of this get yourself a small metal cutting circular saw such as a Bosch or Makita. It really speeds up the job and saves your body. After a while the math gets easy so strive to do the numbers in your head. Avoid coming into the side of any switch boxes. The fittings extend into the box and will obstruct any large size dimmers or timers that you may want to install later, especially if you're going to have a 2 Gang installation. I try to just use top and bottom knockouts everywhere. Switch boxes should be 2 1/8 in deep instead of the standard inch and a half deep 1900 bracket box. They cost a little more but you have more room in the box for dimmer's, timers and more wires that are required with multi-location switches. Believe it or not you can put in 400 or 500 ft 1/2 inch thin wall a day once you're proficient at it. Try to make it look good even though it's going to get covered with drywall. Inspectors love to see good pipe work as it's a key indicator that you know what you're doing.

comments.text:
I'm a first year plumber apprentice and the journeymen that work with me hate me. I rag on how slow they move and how they're teaching me wrong. How they don't take responsibility for directing me leading to errors.


This isn't a career for me, just a job. One day, hopefully soon, I'll be laid off and able to run my side business full time.

Worst points about the apprenticeship. Lazy ass journeymen. I get that apprentices' need to learn how to do the job, but not the housekeeping and moving shit because the journeymen is old, fat, or just straight up lazy. We are a 1:1 team and if we make a mess, we clean it up together.

Journeymen have the final and only words. I break this all the time. No one is going to walk all over me and dismiss critical points I bring up about certain jobs around the site. Everyone always say, "Ask questions" and when I do I'm treated like I won't understand it, or I didn't hear it.

The constant "safety meetings" and the PPE.

Imagine starting a day off. Arriving 15 minutes early and standing around the guys and your journeymen walks up and starts giving you orders. I tell him we aren't on the clock so I can't help him yet. It is now time to work, I grab my tools and his and ask if there is anything else we need and that I will bring it all up for him so we can start working. He will ignore me so I proceed to take our tools and some materials to the work area. I start the daily task plan and he walks up and tells me to hurry. And asks for "XYZ" material that he didn't tell me to get. Then turns walking away grumbling "useless 1st years" or the similar...Now imagine going through that daily while wearing an annoying neck scratching reflective vest. Safety glasses that will fog up hindering your eye sight when doing the most crucial part of the task and a big ass hard hat that slips off, slides down, won't tighten up, gets knocked off from moving around the job.

Yeah...entrepreneurship is my career.

comments.text: Thx for the video.  You mentioned that 18/10 sprinkler wire was used for the control wiring between the generator and the transfer switch.  Most sprinkler wire is rated for 30 Volts (e.g., Southwire's 18/10 sprinkler wire).  If 30 Volt sprinkler wire was used, this is a safety hazard.  Outputs N1, N2, and T1 from the transfer switch are both have a nominal voltage of 120 VAC to ground. Sprinkler wire was used to to carry the voltage of those three 120 VAC control wires. Therefore, this installation is not in accordance with the UL listing of the sprinkler cable (e.g., UL 83) nor is it in accordance with the National Electric Code (NEC), which is formally known as NFPA 70 (e.g., NEC Article 300.3(C)).

Lets check this math real quick. Watts (W) are Volatge (V) * Current (A) , we know that a light bulb is 60W and we also know that US homes run on 120VAC. So let's just plaug that into our little equation there and we get 60 = 120 * A. 7th Grade algebra tells us to find A we divide both sides of the equation by 120. 60/120 = 0.5A or half of an Amp. In the U.S., a bathroom circuit needs to be isolated to a dedicated 20amp circuit. Which means that the circuit cannot have any other loads on it other than the bathroom and a 20amp circuit requires 12 gauge wire minimum. I can't remember the exact year this code was introduced... maybe 2009 or 2012. But I do know that the bathroom GFCI outlet has needed to be on a 20amp circuit for as long as I have been an electrician, which is over 25 years.

comments.author: @Faggledickbob
comments.text: Personally prefer to run 12 gauge everywhere. As of 2017 US NEC 14 is good for up to 20 amps, while 12 is good for up to 30. (Granted that's THHN) Never the less I venture to say that Romex/NM isn't too far behind. It costs a little more, but gives the wire more longevity. As for GFCI breaker on GFCI outlet, I've always been told that you want to avoid that as it can cause complications with the protection. Having the breaker is perfectly suitable, US actually wants us to us Arc fault breakers basically everywhere so some people actually have to get combo breakers. Here in WV things are a lot more relaxed so as long as you're not being stupid about things you can get away with a lot. I would also like to point out that a lot of people don' realize, but boxes have a "fill" that you have to take into consideration when you're laying it out. Yokes (Devices) count as two conductors each. Larger wire means less you can have in the box. Don't think you can run as many conductors into the box as there is holes, people.

comments.author: @Foche_T._Schitt
comments.text:
Not sure where you're located. 
Any US county using 2014/2017 NEC Code calls for no less than one 20 amp GFCI  circuit separate from the lighting which must also be GFCI/AFCI protected.
Modern blow dryer's can pull over 80% of the rating of a #14 wire. 80% is the max continuous load you're allowed to put on a circuit.
(you said you added another circuit but you didn't mention the gauge)

Code also requires a staple every 4.5 feet or less. One staple must be within 8 inches of a plastic box or 12 inches of a metal box.
No more than two circuits under a staple, clamp, or hole. Holes can't be more than 1/3rd the width of the board (centered) or within two inches of another hole. 
Make sure grounds are made up before rough-in inspection.
Make sure lights are rated for a "wet" environment within 3 foot of a shower.

comments.text:
When laying out the boxes, consider how the room will be used and furnished. What seems to be the center of the room when all you see is studs isn't necessarily where the visual center of the room will be once it's furnished. Is that dining light going to be centered over the table? The "six foot rule" -- where no part of a wall can be more than 6 feet from a receptacle -- might not place the receptacles in the exact right spot, so you might have to place some closer than 12 feet apart or only a couple of feet from a doorway in order to not hide them behind a sofa or bed. Try to put overhead lights on a different circuit than the receptacles in the same room, then the room doesn't go dark when you overload the receptacle circuit.

Run conduit from low voltage outlets to the attic or crawl space to facilitate future upgrades. Some new tech WILL come along or you'll need to add connectivity and you'll wish pulling the wires was easier.

comments.text:
Still, how strangely different building codes around the world.
In Russia, we still have the requirement to lay in-wall electrical wiring in metal pipes and corrugated hoses for frame houses. Because the frame house is wooden, that's all. Of course, the strictness of the norms in our country is compensated by the lack of justification for their implementation - we do not have such a strict construction inspection, and we also do not have such a compulsory and comprehensive insurance of real estate (with the attached standards).
However, mortgages and mass construction (over which the supervision is traditionally more careful - but also more prone to bribes than for the activities of individuals) require compromises - and we prefer, for frame houses, open wiring over walls in cable ducts.
Separately, I would like to note that wiring inside the vapor barrier circuit is considered a much more efficient solution. More holes - more water condensation - more risks.

Recommendation: I strongly advise the use of adjustable depth boxes in all locations, but especially for all outlets and switches in the kitchen and bathroom. These rooms most frequently have variable depth wall surfaces when finishes like tile are applied. Instead of having to use a box extender ring, which feels sloppy on new work, or guessing the final finished depth, just use an adjustable depth box.

Doing this for all boxes in an installation adds a very modest upfront cost to the install, but will save both you, your subs and installers, and future contractors and homeowners a lot of minor annoyance (and potentially not insignificant trouble to retrofit).

Client wants thicker drywall? Thicker tile? Decorative paneling over/instead of drywall? Moved a cabinet over an outlet? Accidentally put the box in too deep or too shallow? This is all easily remedied with an adjustable depth box.

comments.author: @scottfurlong5475
comments.text:
The color of the outside sheathing has nothing to do with the size of the wire inside. It's just a color code the manufacturers made up to make it easier for us to identify cables. For example, yellow for #12 120 volt, red for 240 volt, orange for 120/240 volt, blue wire for ArcFault circuits which are required almost everywhere in a home in Canada now and presumably in the US also. I never see him run a single blue cable because he doesn't have to use blue. White colored cable is all over the place with 120v, 120/240v and side #14 on up to very large sizes.
Also, I absolutely cringed when the electrician pushed the panel in between the studs. I hate working on panels that are recessed and we are absolutely not permitted to run our branch circuits through the line side of the panel. We would have to turn the panel upside down. Still, it permanently eliminates many opportunities to bring cable into the panel through the sides.
I did see some pretty interesting stuff in this video. A 200A recessed meter socket detached from the panel connected with what looks like #3/0 copper two conductor cable. Very interesting indeed.

comments.text:
I dislike saddle-boxes because they make it easier for drywallers to hit your wire with their rotozip. I only use them if a slider-box won’t fit in the center.

You can measure from the edges of the door, inspectors will refer to this as a wall-break. All four walls of a room are viewed as one continuous wall. The next outlet can be 12’ from the previous outlet. I also prefer to fold the ground wires to the bottom-left corner before crimping, because it gives you more wire to work with later. That also keeps the grounds next to the neutral terminals, and away from the hot terminals.

Switches can be at a maximum of 48”, for disabled persons and children. They are also best when installed next to doorknobs, when appropriate.

Good looking romex though! I like using the same wire de-spooling method as you, except for homeruns. If you really throw it around it’ll look super slick, and it makes you feel like a cowboy.

comments.author: @dcl97
comments.text:
There is a lot to talk about with this whole full 12ga setup, more than I can write in a youtube comment. 
 I'll just affirm what some others have already said and add that the idea that 14ga is "worse" is fundamentally wrong. It just has a different use case. An old joke amongst electricians is that you can always tell when a homeowner did the wiring because everything is done in 12ga since they think "bigger is better". In some instances it may make sense to do a circuit in 12ga even when not required by code, but in others it may make no sense at all, and cause issues with box fill etc.  Consult your electrician for your specific scenario and I think you'll find a majority dont agree with this concept.

comments.author: @opinionatedman
comments.text:
As an electrician some of this is overkill and some makes sense. For one 12/2 throughout the house is a waste, but the middle ground that has logic is doing the receptacles in 12.  In a brand new home no one should need to plug in portable heaters or window AC units, which are 2 of the biggest culprits I find people overload their circuits with.  Older home's didn't require a 20A bath circuit either. I've seen hair dryers with a wattage label of 1875W, which is more than a whole 15A circuit. Again that's an old home problem in an area already addressed by code. 

A vacuum can draw around 12 amps but it is usually a temporary load. Excluding kitchen/dining/bath areas that already require 20A circuits, most people will never utilize a fraction of any of those 20A circuits. One cost saving route would be to put more receptacles on a circuit. With most lighting going the LED route that's even less load in the system.

Having breakers on the exterior of the house I just hate the idea of it. Main outside if you must; 2020 code when adopted will mandated an exterior shutoff. The whole copper/AL issue has long been settled. Those AL wires will not loosen on those lugs if installed properly, neither will the copper. If the customer wants copper and they got the cash I'm happy to install it, but overall I feel the extra money spent on copper feeders and 12/2 on lighting could have been put to better use elsewhere.

comments.text: Fairly clean layout. While 12/2 or 12/3 is a good idea (despite the issue with tight spots), NO, don't use 20Amp breakers to reduce popping(? breaking). Talking about CAT6E, I know BLE and WiFi is all the rage, but really, look up POE based lighting and other smart home stuff, when those international hackers come calling, they will save your rear. comments.text:
I agree with everything stated in this video, I just wanted to clarify the difference between industry standards/practices and actual NEC requirements. There are electricians out there that can get these subtle differences confused. 

The NEC only specifies insulation color requirements for the neutral (grounded conductor) which is white or gray in color and the EGC (equipment grounding conductor) which is green, green with a yellow stripe. If the EGC is #6 awg or larger bare copper is also permitted.

The marking of ungrounded conductors is an industry standard but can be mandated by local AHU's (authority having jurisdiction).

comments.text: As an audio technician, I need to mention that speakers are wired for low voltage AC signal, and as such, there is no positive or negative, and a speaker doesn’t care which way it is connected. comments.text:
Terrific video. Great method.  I've pulled a lot of wire. I learned a lot (I could've used) from this video. 
For that knot, look for the Magus Hitch (you can also use the Rolling Hitch). Both these hitches have a powerful aspect: When you pull on them they cinch down on the line or wire they're tied to. (Holly of Wind Hippie Sailing had the steel cable backstay on her mast snap in mid ocean. She tied it back down with a rolling hitch. A steel cable. >1000 lbs of force on it.)  The advantage of the Magus Hitch is it's easier to untie later.  
If you tie several knots you might also consider the multi wrap Fisherman's Knot (the one used on the Prusik not the fish hook one)
What's also important, (and obvious to most people, but not to me back in the day....) is when you wrap your electrical tape towards the front as Jacks does here, all the lips of the layers of tape are facing away from the pull.  You won't do it the other way many times before those lips start catching. 
I also like using wax, but I wasn't the guy who knew how to pull wire, I was the guy who learned from guys who knew how to pull wire. So I needed every advantage. 
The last time I snaked anything was in June in the middle of the Pacific Ocean 160 miles south of the Aleutian Islands on top of a sailboat. We had to turn the third reef line (rope) around and run it back through the boom of the mast. No fish wire, just string, (no vacuum - wouldn't have worked anyway.) I used all my wire pulling mojo and a lot of luck. In the end I had to weedle out the para cord (messenger line) from in between a couple of crooked gaps I could not see. Used an aluminum coat hanger  from a hotel in Vietnam. (When my laundry came back, I saw wire and put the hangers right in my sea bag.) When I cut the hanger wire I left it jagged - that's what I snagged the messenger line with.  Had to do this on both ends, was surprised I could do it at all.

No offense but why did you bother converting to Radians? Seems like a wasted step/ time to me unless your taking a Trigonometry class in which case its probably a requirement 🤓

Vpeak = (√2 • Vrms)

RMS (Root Mean Square) is useful when trying to measure the average of numbers, where their sign is unimportant, as the squaring makes all of the numbers non-negative which comes in handy for averaging an alternating waveform 😉

Phase #1 - Vpeak • Sin(θ°)
Phase #2 - Vpeak • Sin(θ° - 120°) 
Phase #3 - Vpeak • Sin(θ° - 240°)

You can enter this into a TI graphing calculator to visually verify how this shifts the waveforms along the x-axis, just make sure you in Degree mode and not Radians ☺

Law of Cosines 
---------------------------
c² = a² + b² - 2abCos(θ°) 
a = 120Vrms
b = 120Vrms
θ° = 60° (Phase - Neutral)
θ° = 120° (Phase - Phase)

c = √[120² + 120² - 2•(120)•(120) • Cos(60°)] = √[14400] = 120Vrms ( Wye Phase - Neutral ) 🤔
c = √[120² + 120² - 2•(120)•(120) • Cos(120°)] = √[43200] = 207.85Vrms ( ≈ 208Vrms) ( Wye Phase - Phase )😊

Great videos! However US residential electric is 240 V - the difference is that we use transformers with a center tap. The main panel in most homes has two 120v legs plus a neutral that is connected to the center tap. So in the panel a connection from one leg to neutral ( connected to center tap)  yields 120v and a connection across both legs is 240. 
The confusion is that most circuits, and appliances are 120v. However most homes have electric clothes dryers, stoves, water heaters, central AC or similar that use 240 circuits. 
I believe the confusion is that many other systems don’t use center tapped transformers…. At I believe this is true of the UK.

comments.author: @BaldurKhr
comments.text:
At 5:02 when N is facing the upper coil, something else happens. When the N pole is right in front of the coil, emf=0 ! There is no current.
Explanation : 
As the N pole approached the upper coil, the magnetic flux through it was increasing so current was generated in one direction, but now as the N pole is moving away from the coil, the magnetic flux is decreasing so current will switch the flowing direction !!! Its all about dPhi/dt ( change in mag flux). It is not dependent on the intensity of the field lines in the coil, but in the change of the field lines through the coil. Therefore in between these increase and decrease of m. flux, the current is assumed to be 0 ( ideally, if no self inductance is taken into account). Maximum current through the coil is obtained when N and S are perpendicular to the coils, that’s when phi varies the most.
Despite this small detail, i found your vid very useful. 
Thanks a lot for all your videos, they’re of great value! All the best!

comments.text:
I wire mostly residential in SC, and back in 2015 when I started my apprenticeship, the electricians that taught me had worked as a subcontractor that get paid by the job and therefore using the daisy chain method because it allowed for a speedier installation, and so for myself, I typically use the daisy chain method, ONLY by using the screw terminals, NEVER the backstab wiring.  Those backstabs however guarantee me a fairly steady cash flow when I do service work as my other part time job 😊

I also use the pigtail method a lot as well.  Usually because there are more than two cables entering the box that connect to the receptacle.   I also deal with multiwire branch circuits A LOT when doing commercial/industrial, some which involve 277 volt twist lock receptacles for high bay lighting and so forth. In these cases since the neutral is required to be pigtailed, I just go the extra mile and figure I might as well go ahead and pigtail the hot as well.   

A few weeks ago I went on a service call where a TV, Blu-ray player, DVR, stereo system and computer filled the living room with smoke,  surge protector caught fire, a few light bulbs blew out, other lights were very dim.  Home was built in 1991,  and used multwire circuits in the living room/master bed, downstairs rec room and kitchen, no handle ties on any of the breakers except for the 240V appliance circuits. The first receptacle on the circuit burned out at the neutral side which was backstabbed.  

I'm guessing pigtail the neutral on a multiwire circuit wasn't required in 1991, nor were hand ties.  The oldest NEC book I have is 2014 and even it has all these requirements.   

If anyone has any historical knowledge of the NEC I'd be interested to learn more about the history regarding requirements for multiwire circuits. So far the limited info I found online points me to 2008 NEC for the handle tie requirement, prior to that the handle tie was only required if both ungrounded conductors landed on the same device yoke.

comments.author: @davenag957
comments.text: Like you, I have been in the electrical trade a long time. My first code book is from 1978. In those years I've worked in residential, commercial, industrial manufacturing and chemical wet processing environments.  I've seen countless failures of all sorts of devices and equipment. Most of those failures are from either poor installation practices or environmental degradation. The equipment is normally not the culprit. Loose and improperly made connections is number one. Moisture, humidity or chemical attack is number two. The listing agencies and code commitees go over the top to guarantee safety. Devices and splicing components are tested way beyond the loads they are rated for. Its all up to the installer to use these products correctly. As soon as I open an electrical box when troubleshooting, the workmanship, or lack of, tells me what I will need to look for throughout the rest of the installation. Wire nuts falling off, loose device screws, loose boxes, loose locknuts, lack of proper grounding, short wires, etc. The human factor part of the installation is the variable, which is THE hardest part of the equation to solve. With all that said, I would recommend pigtailing the devices, as I feel it will hold up the longest in the real world. Most installers/DIYers don't have a torque screwdriver and dont tighten the device screws properly, leading to overheating and ultimate failure. If the screws aren't tight, they will loosen as the device is being pushed into the box. At that point, the downstream load will begin the degradation process leading to failure of the entire circuit, instead of just the one device.

comments.author: @BuddyTobyTV
comments.text:
I think there’s another big issue not covered here. I’m not an electrician but handy homeowner. I’ve seen twice an outlet get hot at the connection tab or thereabouts on pass through. In one case, it was very close to starting a fire. 

The cause seemed to be just that the outlet was old and this somewhat corroded and dirty. That tab and connection point is relatively more exposed but hidden behind the cover plate. Still it will collect dust or corrode with time. 

I’ve never pulled a decades old wirenut to see burning and melted plastic. Dust just doesn’t seem to get into a proper wire but connection. 

I agree with the video, but I would add this for good practice. I wouldn’t do pass through for more than one or two outlets if at all possible. 

Don’t take a string of 6,7,8 outlets and daisy chain them. That is begging someone to plug in a heavy load device 25 years in the future on the outlet 6th in the line and cause the tab and gunk on the outlet 2nd in line to get really hot. 

My suggestions:
Do a pigtail unless it’s not easily/feasibly done (small/shallow box, GFCI/AFCI, etc.)
If downstream is to a new room/area, do a pigtail on all connections before that room or pigtail a depart branch for the other room or area. 
If time is an issue, consider using wagos or other connectors. 
Don’t do a pass through more than two times in a row. 
Don’t have more than 3 outlets fed off a pass through. So if it’s a long series, only do pass through in the second to last and maybe third to last. Alternatively, make 3-4 outlet branches so you don’t get so many in a row. You want to minimize the number of connections between the receptacle and the panel. 
For pass throughs, cover the screws and tan with electrical tape to help keep dust dirty and moisture off. 

Again I am not an electrician. Am engineer but not of the sparky kind.

comments.author: @pibbles-a-plenty1105
comments.text: It all boils down to Ohm's Law, not YOUTUBE Master Electrician.  Through wiring, if done properly, has a constant insertion resistance, each terminal adding to the wire run resistance.  Pig tail junctions, if done properly, add LESS resistance at each junction - the receptacle terminal resistance is out of the equation.  The bottom line is about voltage drop along a branch.  The number of receptacles in a branch must be limited to prevent too much voltage drop so that loads are provided adequate operating voltage under high branch loading conditions.  Think Ohm's Law, not Elmer Fudd's coin toss method.

comments.author: @tizzy6
comments.text:
-Strip 16” all wires
-Cut out center strands leaving a few outside strands
-Use a few strands from each side of individual conductors, cut away excess
Fold strands through eye of rope from opposing side while staggering each wire as to allow each cut out to sit inside each other as you get to eye.
Cut excess wires in staggering formation 
Tape tight, if done well, there will be no bumps, puts or ridges to get caught up on.

comments.author: @MB-zj3er
comments.text: I use a rope with a multiple loop bowline to stagger my conductors. Then, as others have said, I keep 3 or four strands from both sides of the OUTSIDE of each conductor which keeps you from creating snags like you have. Then fold them over each individual loop from opposite sides. And last tip, do your first wrap of tape with the adhesive side out, and then overwrap as normal. Now when your pull is done you can just run a razor knife down the head and the tape will literally fall off.

comments.author: @WW-hr1hd
comments.text:
The illustration at 2:54 is confusing.  Assuming that the black wire is the hot wire, the white is the neutral, and the green is the ground, the illustration makes it appear as if the ground wire between the GFCI receptacle and the regular receptacle is the "Load" wire, and that the hot (black) wire between the panel and the GFCI receptacle is the "Line" wire.

It should be made clear that "Line" refers to the "set" of wires coming into the GFCI from the panel, and "Load" refers to the "set" of wires leading from the GFCI to the regular receptacle.  The black wire coming from the panel needs to be attached to the hot line terminal on the GFCI , and the white wire needs to be attached to the GFCI's neutral line terminal.

Then the black wire leading from the GFCI to the regular receptacle needs to be attached to the hot load terminal on the GFCI, and the white wire needs to be attached to the neutral load terminal on the GFCI.

There is only one ground terminal on a GFCI receptacle since "Line" and "Load" only apply to the current-carrying wires, not the ground wire.

comments.author: @bobpond7973
comments.text: IMPORTANT:  Leviton GFCI's have "Line" terminals at the top. The model shown in this video (including the wiring diagram shown) has line terminals at the bottom.  At 3:35 in the video you note something like "If you are replacing an old GFCI with a new GFCI then it is easier to do as you just place the wires from the line terminals of the old GFCI onto the line terminals of the new GFCI."  Strictly speaking this is correct, but only if you use a voltage tester or actually read the labels on the back of the old GFCI and the new GFCI.  If you are unfortunate, your old GFCI may have the line terminals on the top while your new GFCI has the line terminals on the bottom.  If this is the case and you simply move the top wires from the old GFCI to the top terminals of the new GFCI and move the bottom wires from the old to the bottom terminals of the new then the LED of the GFCI will light up green, suggesting that it is active, but the GFCI will not reset, the outlet itself will not be live and the downstream circuit will not be live.  You may then think that you have to call an electrician to track down a (non-existant) ground fault. The bottom line (no pun intended):  when wiring a GFCI, you MUST read the labels on the back of the outlet (or read the installation instructions that come with the new GFCI) and make sure to connect the live wire from the panel and the neutral coming from the panel onto the terminals marked "line" on the back of the new GFCI outlet.

comments.author: @fldave612
comments.text: Unless the codes where you are located differ from the NEC, that ground wire should have ran from the grounding electrodes and into your meter can first, it gets bonded to the neutral in the meter can, then ran from  the meter can to your breaker panel.  You would bond it to the neutral in your garage panel ONLY if that your main panel (first point of disconnect).  I noticed someone else mentioned the intersystems bonding termination, that is also a code requirement as of the 2008 NEC on all residential installations.   As far as securing the pull elbow to the wall, you got a few options.  1. Drill small pilot holes inside the box and secure it with stainless screws to the sheathing, since that elbow doesn't have any current carrying conductors I don't think an inspector will have an issue with this, but certainly check with the building department for sure before doing it.  2. You could get a pull elbow with screw "ears" on them and again use stainless screws to fasten it.  3. If you're crafty, you could secure your riser sweep to the structure just below the box with a conduit clamp to secure the bottom of the elbow, then glue a male thread fitting into the exit side of the elbow, cut a 4x4" section of 3/4" plywood as a backer to hole you drilled in the sheathing, make sure only the threads of fitting protrude through both the sheathing and the backer, then thread a locknut onto it to secure the top of the elbow.   Lastly, I would pack some silicone behind the elbow filling the voids where it goes through the hole in the siding/sheathing, trust me water will  find its way in and slowly rot that that sheathing, if you choose the method of driving a screw through the elbow and into the siding, pack silicone behind it for sure.

comments.author: @naturetruth5218
comments.text:
Is it not a bad idea to connect main supply Neutral to Earth that many utility company warn against? Shorting Neutral directly to Earth, it make the Neutral a Earth.

If the Neutral is not ideally ZERO voltage potential due to 3 Phase power imbalance loading, there will be constant current flowing in the earth wire. With bad earthing (resistance above 5 ohms), you might always get slight electric shock in appliances metal casing connected to earth wire.

Earth wire should be joined to the Earth rail, not Neutral rail. Then connect to the metal panel box to earth the box for safety. The whole house earth wiring is then connect to the Earth Rail ONLY, not neutral.

Lastly, its important you verify the earth is working with resistance ideally below 5ohms for home usage, or below 2ohms for more heavy usage. Use a Three points earth measuring meter, or at least ensure a electric appliance of 2KW connected to 220V supply has a minimum 8A current flowing through the earth wire (110V is 16A) if connect to LIVE wire and Earth directly (instead of Neutral).

Otherwise, you may ended with a bad earthing of 50~300 ohms giving false security and not well protected. 

From the video poor dry sand stone soil condition without treating with salts and charcoal to provide extra moisture, your earth resistance of two 2m rods space 2m apart might be 20~100ohms, increasing to 50~200ohms during dry summer unless you wet the surrounding soil regularly. So you should test the resistance, if need to, add extra earth rods, select a moisture area of good soil for better conductivity.

Our body resistance is 300ohms when wet, 1000ohms when dry. Hence for a 30A main supply, a 10A current can still flow from faulty water heater through your body while showering is not very pleasant.

comments.author: @deepredstate4414
comments.text: Very good job on install however you installed a Victron DC to DC converter NOT a charger. The difference is the converter stabilizes the DC for sensitive electronics but is usually used to CONVERT two different voltages like 24v to 12v etc. The other main issue is that it does NOT regulate current for the Lithium batteries. Whereas the the DC to DC Charger has battery charge protocols for Lithium ( three stage charging) that regulate the current to prevent damaging the alternator. The Converter is not INTENDED for use as a charger. Also if you are grounding the devices to chassis ground then you can save money and buy the NON isolated version.

comments.author: @whatimhearingusayis9379
comments.text:
If it was me I would use a gfci outlet for every outlet. These detect a difference in currents going out of and returning to the receptacle ( .04-.06 milliamperes typically) this way if an appliance faults it won’t become energized
    The term used by electricians for the connectors used to connect a SO/SOOW cable assembly or single wire in to a box/housing/panel is often referred to as a CGB vs your term “gland” in case someone needs to get an extra one at an electrical supply house. I am impressed with your simple to follow, rudimentary, accurate and  step by step instruction and installation of this electrical system. My only extra advice is that there are good reasons for having a manual disconnect switch for every portion of the integrated system especially when troubleshooting or servicing or if a component of the system fails. Perhaps these disconnect switches could be installed just outside of the main battery/inverter compartment in case of a fire. I also like the idea of having the system in a steel or aluminum box ( I realize this could effect Bluetooth connections maybe the dongle could be mounted just outside of it)It will probably never have a catastrophic incident however if it did it a high amperage fault could be ugly. One last thing normally residential/commercial breaker panels are made by a specific manufacturer and typically the panels are UL listed to have only there own brand and model of breaker used in that panel. I noticed you used a Square D single pole 50 amp as well as some Siemens tandem 20 amp breakers in the same 120 volt breaker box. Are both of these brands approved for use in it?  I bring this up because I have seen insurance company’s try to deny customer insurance claims because different breakers were used in homes.  If I may also recommend insure when you set a clamp ( your shore power socket) that it is on top of the outer Romex insulation/jacketing, otherwise great job.

comments.text:
Absolutely amazing video, simple explanation of a very complex install, WOW!

2 concerns
1) The minute you made the connection on the roof to the solar panels you were working with live wires, would have been better to connect to isolator first then panels.
2) The connection to the van battery, should be done via an ignition switched relay, so it only energizes when the engine is running, to prevent drawing down your start battery while parked. 
You have essentially added your start battery to your house bank and if you ever draw it down you won't be able to start the van.

Again amazing video, I am currently considering my own off grid build, and the solar idea has been very intimidating, not anymore, Thank You.

comments.author: @srira7910
comments.text: Hey Lauren, this is such a great production!  With 4 LFP batteries, would suggest replacing the fuse off that bank with a T-Class fuse instead. LFP batteries have very low resistance, and thus, can deliver very high amounts of current. In the event of a short or failure, you want a fuse with a much higher AIC (Amp Interrupting Capacity) rating than an ANL fuse. Otherwise you risk the fuse melting into itself, which would offer no protection, and a risk of a serious fire... The ABYC marine standards suggest the proper fuse for LiFePO4 is a Class T fuse. This is due to the 20,000A AIC rating of the Class T fuse.

comments.author: @flawmore
comments.text:
Here is some bonus info from an electrician from another country.
Every installed thing has a leak current, which is normal. But if too many devices are running through the same RCCB, it can add up to the point where it trips, even though there is no short circuit anywhere. A rare thing, but when it happens it's likely in a place like a restaurant kitchen or similar, where they have machinery that consumes a lot of power running over the same RCCB. Good to know if you end up in this situation, it may not be the first thing that comes to mind. Recommended max MCBs per RCCB where I live is 9. And that is for a normal household.

comments.author: @netking66
comments.text:
I can assure you trying to find a fault in an old paper insulated lead sheathed underground 230/400 volt cable is no fun. A 300A or 400A fuse blows, there is a 'no power' complaint, the faultman puts in a new fuse link which holds for 10 minutes and it goes again. Testing gives indecisive results (modern test equipment may help). You are in for hours with irate customers hanging around. You may need to ensure each customers' terminations are disconnected and some may be behind locked doors and no key. Several years ago in London there were five such failures on one cable over several days - they thought they had it fixed but it was not - that negatively impacted fault statistics - cable systems are far more reliable in aggregate than overhead lines.
By comparison finding a similar fault in a 11,000 volt cable is a piece of cake.

comments.author: @voidwareprohibited
comments.text: You desperately need to fuse that 12v cable coming off the vehicle battery, at the battery. If you rub through that cable and short between your breaker and the vehicle battery, your build is toast. You should also ideally use some flexible conduit on that battery cable. This cable  to your DCDC charger is generally tied in to the vehicle fuse box under the drivers feet. It's a Mini ANL fuse, and there's an open position. You can exit under the front floor, there's a cable run, feed it into the drivers seat pedestal, and out the factory floor boot.

comments.author: @cknox64
comments.text:
If the "wire highway" is to get power from one side to the other, why not run the supply mains to one or more fuse boxes then branch out along that side from there? Fewer wires under the van.

I would also recommend the plug (male) connectors on the device with the outlet (female) on the supply side, like the appliances in your house. And, make one lead longer than the other. For instance, make the hot longer, perhaps by 1/4" to 1/2", from the device and the ground longer, by the same length, from the supply. Not only will this help keep polarity straight if you need to unplug something, but the connectors won't be side-by-side.

I like the cabinetry skills.

comments.author: @jmac213stuff
comments.text: @3:58. "For 12-2 you have to put that into a 3/4" Conduit." It not correct. Looking at the Romex specification chart, 14-2 is .368x.162, and 12-2 is .418x.179. These are the two smallest Romex cables and basically, looking at the 53% Fill from table 4, Chapter 9, for 3/4 is .283 and for 1" is .458, so both 14-2  (.368) or 12-2(.418) in 3/4" doesn't meet code. For Romex to be in ENT, it needs to be 1" (.458) or larger.

comments.text: Nice job and great explanation. And after you ensure there is no voltage between the Ground and Neutral (top and right side), set your multimeter to the Ohms scale to ensure there is CONTINUITY between the two lead) - just seeing that there is no voltage reading doesn't mean the wires are actually connected to anything. comments.text:
Interesting, 2000 hours of off the job training. Do you know how much of that is face to face learning and how much is “self directed” learning? In Australia we typically run an electrical trades certificate 3 (trade certificate) qualification for 3 years. 36 weeks per year, 8 hours per week = 864 nominal in class hours. To meet the nominal hours for a certificate 3 in Australia, we specify many hundreds of hours of “self directed” learning which means homework effectively. This homework is usually not enforced or counted towards any grades. I’d really appreciate any details on how the electrical trades course runs overseas. I feel the Australian qualifications are glorified as being prestigious, but they are not what they used to be and we are in real need of a wake up call! Any details like a course code or a website that contains the curriculum would be fantastic so I can begin some research. 

By the way our apprenticeships are a nominal 4 years, 4 days per week on site at 8 hours per day = 1536 hours per year while you study, plus the final year being 5 days per week, 8 hours per day = around 1920 hours. So in total approximately 6,500 hours of on site experience.
